title: India's Cash Paradox: Currency in Circulation Keeps Growing Despite UPI Boom
excerpt: The RBI finds cash demand increasingly harder to predict as digital payments surge, with rupee banknotes in circulation now exceeding ₹41 trillion even as UPI processes billions of transactions monthly.
body:
• India's currency in circulation reached ₹41.23 trillion in FY26, up 11.9% year-on-year, even as UPI transactions hit record highs with over 22 billion transactions per month.
  • The RBI describes this as the "currency demand paradox" — digital payments are substituting transactional cash use, but precautionary and store-of-value motives keep total currency growing.
  • The ₹500 note now accounts for 85.5% of all banknotes in circulation by value, suggesting Indians are hoarding large denominations while using UPI for everyday purchases.

India's central bank is grappling with an increasingly unpredictable cash economy. Despite the explosive growth of UPI and digital payments, the total value of rupee banknotes in circulation has continued to rise steadily — a phenomenon the Reserve Bank of India calls the "currency demand paradox."

The value of banknotes in circulation climbed 11.9% to ₹41.23 trillion in fiscal year 2026, according to the RBI. That's roughly three times the value of U.S. dollar bills in circulation on a per-capita basis, and it's growing faster than many economists expected given India's digital payments revolution.

Two Economies in One

The numbers tell the story of a country running two parallel payment systems. UPI processed over 22.3 billion transactions worth ₹29 lakh crore in April 2026, according to National Payments Corporation of India data. The platform now handles roughly 85% of India's retail digital payments, and the average ticket size has plunged from ₹3,867 in 2016-17 to just ₹1,404 in 2024-25 — evidence that even micro-payments have gone digital.

Yet cash keeps piling up. An RBI research paper titled "Cash versus Digital Payment Transactions in India: Decoding the Currency Demand Paradox" found that while the transactional use of cash is declining, the precautionary and store-of-value motives for holding physical currency remain deeply entrenched.

"Cash is still the king... though UPI is gaining traction."

— SBI Research

This is reflected in the denomination mix. The ₹500 note accounts for 85.5% of total banknotes by value. Growth in currency circulation has been "primarily driven by the demand for large-denomination banknotes," the RBI paper noted, while smaller notes have seen declining share — partly because UPI and mobile wallets have substituted small-value payments.

Why Cash Persists

Several factors explain why Indians continue to stockpile cash even as they tap their phones to pay for chai. Research by SBI economists published in Mint identified four key drivers.

First, a chilling effect from tax enforcement. In July 2025, Karnataka's Commercial Taxes Department issued roughly 18,000 GST notices to small traders for UPI transactions exceeding the ₹40 lakh registration threshold. Statistical analysis showed that districts with higher prior ATM activity experienced significant increases in cash withdrawals after the notices, a pattern that extended to West Bengal and Kerala — suggesting the crackdown pushed some merchants back to cash.

Second, low bank deposit rates and rising rural consumption have increased the motivation to hold cash rather than park money in savings accounts. Third, surging gold and silver prices have led some households to liquidate precious metals for cash. Fourth, the RBI's directive to increase ₹100 and ₹200 denomination notes in ATMs after the ₹2,000 note withdrawal has boosted lower-denomination circulation.

The Diaspora Angle

For NRIs who remember the chaos of demonetization in 2016, India's cash resilience might seem counterintuitive. The country that leapfrogged card payments to build the world's most successful real-time payments system still can't wean itself off paper. The cash-to-GDP ratio has declined from 14.4% in the pandemic year of 2020-21 to 11.2% in 2025-26, indicating a gradual shift, but the absolute volume of currency keeps climbing.

Digital payments as a share of GDP have surged past 800%, recording a compound annual growth rate of 48% by volume and 12.5% by value over the past decade, according to the RBI's study on UPI's impact on cash demand. ATM cash withdrawals as a share of GDP have fallen steadily since 2018-19.

What's Next

The RBI is taking a dual approach. It plans a phased rollout of banknotes with upgraded security features starting mid-2026, signaling that physical currency remains a core priority. Its Central Bank Digital Currency (CBDC) initiative, however, remains nascent — circulation stands at just ₹1,016 crore, or 0.02% of total currency in circulation.

The upshot: India's payment landscape is not a story of cash versus digital, but of both growing simultaneously in a $4 trillion economy that is still formalizing. The RBI's challenge is managing monetary policy when the cash portion of that equation becomes increasingly difficult to forecast.
